steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transformers have been used for mathematics problems, both symbolic and numerical. But they have trouble with basic arithmetic. Large language models (LLM) can learn addition or multiplication by a small prefactor, and they generalize beyond their training range when they are fine-tuned with scratchpad, chain-of-thought or algorithmic prompting, but these techniques need bespoke data and they do not extend to complex tasks. Math transformers were also found to be brittle, to fail on simple tasks, and to be hard to interpret, except in the simplest cases. On the other hand small transformers can learn advanced calculations like eigen-decomposition and polynomial roots.

In this paper I train 4 -layer transformers to compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers, which is an important operation for rational arithmetic and number theory. I observe that:

- 1. Transformers learn to cluster input pairs that have the same GCD. All pairs of integers (a,b) with the same GCD k get the same prediction.

- 2. Transformer predictions can be fully characterized. In training the model learns a set of integers \mathcal{D}, and for any input pair (a,b) it predicts the largest element in \mathcal{D} that divides a and b.

- 3. Early in training, transformers learn to predict products of divisors of the base used to represent integers. Small primes are "grokked" after extended training.

- 4. log-uniform operands and outcomes -> better performance; up to 91 GCD \leq 100 correct; predictions still fully explainable
- 5. unbalanced outcome distribution needed for full explainability; partially fails with uniformly distributed GCD
- impact: exact calculations with integer divisibility; three directions (explainability approach; log-uniform distributions for other arithmetic tasks, e.g. fine tuning LLM; Foundational Models for Science, high energy physics, computational biology, astrophysics); before they can do science, transformers must learn maths

## Related work
- neural nets for arithmetic first proposed by early work, recurrent models; fine-tuning LLM for math word problems; summary; NALUs (weights near 0, 1 or -1)
- hardness: factorization hard in a benchmark; modular arithmetic; extending four-operation results to GCD and Euclid's algorithm
- number representation; grokking (first description, metrics, feed-forward analysis); explainability via model weights; similar experiments for linear algebra

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformers have been used for mathematics problems, both symbolic and numerical. But they have trouble with basic arithmetic. Large language models (LLM) can learn addition or multiplication by a small prefactor, and they generalize beyond their training range when they are fine-tuned with scratchpad, chain-of-thought or algorithmic prompting, but these techniques need bespoke data and they do not extend to complex tasks. Math transformers were also found to be brittle, to fail on simple tasks, and to be hard to interpret, except in the simplest cases. On the other hand small transformers can learn advanced calculations like eigen-decomposition and polynomial roots.

In this paper I train 4 -layer transformers to compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers, which is an important operation for rational arithmetic and number theory. I observe that:

- 1. Transformers learn to cluster input pairs that have the same GCD. All pairs of integers (a,b) with the same GCD k get the same prediction.

- 2. Transformer predictions can be fully characterized. In training the model learns a set of integers \mathcal{D}, and for any input pair (a,b) it predicts the largest element in \mathcal{D} that divides a and b.

- 3. Early in training, transformers learn to predict products of divisors of the base used to represent integers. Small primes are "grokked" after extended training.

- 4. Models that are trained from log-uniform operands and outcomes have better performance. They predict up to 91 GCD \leq 100 correctly. The model predictions are still fully explainable.

- 5. For full explainability you need an unbalanced distribution of outcomes in the training set: explainability partially fails when models are trained from uniformly distributed GCD.

These results show that transformers can be trained to do exact calculations involving integer divisibility, which is a central task in integer arithmetic and number theory. The research also has a broader potential impact beyond GCD, in three directions. First, it is a new approach to model explainability: black-box model predictions are fully characterized by experimenting with selected inputs and using our theoretical understanding of the mathematics underneath. Second, the results on log-uniform training distributions of operands and outcomes (faster learning and better performance) may extend to other arithmetic tasks, e.g. fine tuning LLM. Finally, mathematical tasks are central for Foundational Models for Science, which are large language models pre-trained on mathematics and fine-tuned on specific fields, like high energy physics, computational biology or astrophysics. Transformers must learn maths before they can do science.

## Related work

Neural networks for arithmetic were first proposed by early work, and recurrent models were proposed in later work. Most recent research focuses on fine-tuning LLM on arithmetic tasks to solve math word problems. There is a summary in another paper. Another alternative is Neural Arithmetic Logical Units, which learn exact computations that can generalize to any input, by constraining the weights of linear models to be close to 0, 1 or -1.

Many authors discussed how hard it is to learn arithmetic tasks. One benchmark of mathematical tasks observes that number theoretic operations, like factorization, are hard. Another work looks further into the hardness of modular arithmetic. Others note that it is difficult to extend the promising results obtained by previous work on the four operations to complex mathematical calculations or algorithms, here GCD and Euclid's algorithm.

The role of number representation was discussed in earlier work. Grokking was first described by prior work. Some authors propose metrics to characterize it. Another paper gives an insightful analysis of grokking in feed-forward networks. Most prior work on explainability in arithmetic transformers tries to interpret model weights. Earlier work does similar experiments for linear algebra.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformers [1] have been applied to problems of mathematics, both symbolic [2,3,4] and numerical [5]. Yet, they struggle with basic arithmetic [6,7]. Large language models (LLM) can learn addition or multiplication by a small prefactor, and generalize beyond their training range when fine-tuned using scratchpad [8], chain-of-thought [9] or algorithmic prompting [10], but these techniques require bespoke data and do not extend to complex tasks [11]. Math transformers were also found to be brittle [12], to fail on simple tasks [13], and to be hard to interpret, except in the simplest cases [14]. Still, small transformers can learn advanced calculations, such as eigen-decomposition [5] and polynomial roots [15].

In this paper, I train 4 -layer transformers to compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers, an important operation for rational arithmetic and number theory, and observe that:

- 1. Transformers learn to cluster input pairs with the same GCD. All pairs of integers (a,b) with the same GCD k are predicted the same.

- 2. Transformer predictions can be fully characterized. During training, the model learns a set of integers \mathcal{D}, and predicts, for any input pair (a,b), the largest element in \mathcal{D} that divides a and b.

- 3. Early in training, transformers learn to predict products of divisors of the base used to represent integers. Small primes are "grokked" [16] after extended training.

- 4. Models trained from log-uniform operands and outcomes perform better. They correctly predict up to 91 GCD \leq 100. Model predictions remain fully explainable.

- 5. Full explainability requires an unbalanced distribution of outcomes in the training set: explainability partially fails once models are trained from uniformly distributed GCD.

These results show how transformers can be trained to perform exact calculations involving integer divisibility, a central task in integer arithmetic and number theory. Beyond GCD calculations, the broader potential impact of this research extends in three directions. First, it presents a new approach to model explainability: fully characterizing black-box model predictions by experimenting with selected inputs and using our theoretical understanding of the underlying mathematics. Second, the results on log-uniform training distributions of operands and outcomes – faster learning and better performance – may extend to other arithmetic tasks, e.g. fine tuning LLM. Finally, mathematical tasks play a central role for Foundational Models for Science – large language models pre-trained on mathematics, and fine-tuned on specific fields, such as high energy physics, computational biology or astrophysics. Before they can do science, transformers must learn maths.

## Related work

Neural networks for arithmetic were first proposed by [17], and recurrent models by [18], [19] and [20]. Recent research mostly focuses on fine-tuning LLM on arithmetic tasks, to solve math word problems [21,22]. See [6] for a summary. As an alternative, Neural Arithmetic Logical Units [23,24] learn exact computations that can generalize to any input, by constraining the weights of linear models to be close to 0, 1 or -1.

The difficulty of learning arithmetic tasks was discussed by many authors. [25], benchmarking mathematical tasks, observe that number theoretic operations, like factorization, are hard. [26] further investigates the hardness of modular arithmetic. [11] note how difficult it is to extend the promising results obtained by [6] on the four operations to complex mathematical calculations or algorithms – here, GCD and Euclid's algorithm.

The role of number representation was discussed by [7] and [5]. Grokking was first described by [16], and [27] propose metrics to characterize it. [28] provides an insightful analysis of grokking in feed-forward networks. Most prior work on explainability in arithmetic transformers tries to interpret model weights [14,29]. [30] conducts similar experiments for linear algebra.
